Rules and guidelines from the book
One ACL per interface, per protocol, per direction.
You can have one inbound and one outbound IP ACL on an interface. A second one replaces the first. Two lists in the same direction would make the second useless, because of the implicit deny.

New lines go at the bottom.

A packet matches line 3 of a 6-line ACL. What happens to lines 4 to 6?
They are not checked - the router acts on the first match and stops.
A packet matches no line in an ACL. What happens to it?
It is dropped - the implicit deny at the end drops it.
. What happens to a packet from 10.2.2.2?
Denied - it matches no line, so the implicit deny applies.
Which number creates a standard IP ACL?
A - standard is 1-99 and 1300-1999. 100-199 is extended. 2700 is outside the ranges.
Which number creates an extended IP ACL?
B - extended is 100-199 and 2000-2699. 99 and 1450 are standard. 2750 is outside the range.
A standard ACL can match which part of a packet?
A - standard ACLs check the source IP address only.
Why can you not permit only web traffic to one server with a standard ACL?
It cannot see the destination or port - only an extended ACL checks destination, protocol and port.
Where should you normally place an extended ACL that blocks Telnet from LAN A to LAN B?
On the interface closest to LAN A, inbound - extended ACLs go near the source so unwanted traffic is dropped early.
